extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, literature students, and critics studying classical poetics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and evaluating tragic and epic poetry (and related imitative arts), focusing on plausibility, diction, unity, treatment of the unnatural, and how to answer critical objections. Draws on Aristotle's Poetics and classical critical practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer a plausible impossibility to an unconvincing possibility
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'plausible impossibility' is poetically preferable to an 'unconvincing possibility'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an element is impossible in fact but yields the required poetic effect (the marvellous, correspondence), it can be acceptable; conversely, a merely possible event that fails to convince harms the poetry. (Example references: bath-scene, appearance of a ghost; the notion that the improbable tends to occur.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid making the account out of unaccountable elements
rubrics_metrics.description: The account should not be constructed from unaccountable (unnatural) elements as an integral part of the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the fiction would have failed without such unaccountable features, their presence is illegitimate. When unnatural elements are necessary, they should not be required from the outset; otherwise the story is defective (example: Electra's report of the Pythian Games as anachronism).

rubrics_metrics.name: If employing the unnatural, either keep it in background or prepare/emphasize it
rubrics_metrics.description: When a poet decides to use unnatural elements, two acceptable approaches exist: keep them in the background or else fully emphasize and prepare the audience for them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rottéken's rule: if the poet employs the unnatural, it is better to emphasize it and thoroughly prepare the hearer rather than let it stand unexplained in the foreground; otherwise conceal or background it (examples: Oedipus's ignorance vs Pythian Games).

rubrics_metrics.name: Special care with diction in 'flat' passages; avoid over‑brilliant diction
rubrics_metrics.description: In passages lacking psychology or reasoning ('flat' passages), diction should be handled with special care; over-brilliant diction obscures psychology and reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the principle of economical employment of means: use the minimal effective linguistic means. Over-elaborate language can hide the mental processes or arguments the passage should convey.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accommodate diction to character
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction must be suited to the character portrayed; poetical diction is not uniform across characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grandiloquence is unsuitable for humble characters. Poetic licence exists, but diction should reflect rank, station, and character so the portrayal is believable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portray one of three types: the real, the traditional (conventional), or the ideal
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet, as portrayer, depicts either the real (past or present), the traditional/conventional, or the ideal (type).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These modes may be expressed in ordinary language or via dialectic words and metaphors. Idealizing the type is permissible where it serves poetic ends; depart from reality only when the advantages outweigh disadvantages (examples: statues of rulers idealized).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish poetical correctness from other correctnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetical correctness is not identical with correctness of other disciplines (moral, scientific, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetical incorrectness may be (a) inability on the artist’s part to portray as intended, or (b) wrong election/choice (e.g., portraying a horse incorrectly), or violation of some other science. If the fiction attains its poetic end, some incorrectness can be acceptable; but if accuracy in the other science would not have impeded the poetic effect, there is harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess errors by their relation to the art’s immediate concern
rubrics_metrics.description: Errors are lighter if they concern matters external to the art itself and heavier if they affect the art's immediate portrayal or likeness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: it is a lighter error for a painter not to know that a hind is hornless than to paint it so that it does not resemble a hind. Judge the severity by whether the mistake undermines the portrayal’s resemblance or function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defend departures from truth by idealization, tradition, or factual representation
rubrics_metrics.description: When criticized as untrue, the poet may reply that characters are idealized, that the matter is traditional/conventional, or that the depiction, though unedifying, represents factual practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Sophocles' characters described as ideal; Homeric theology defended as tradition; description of spears stuck erect defended as representing period practice or foreign custom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge propriety of utterance/performance by context (subject, object, occasion, beneficiary, purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: The appropriateness of an utterance or performance must be judged not abstractly but relative to its subject, object, occasion, beneficiary, and purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A line or action may be proper in one context and improper in another; criticism must attend to the intended purpose or advantage/detriment being addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolve apparent inconsistencies by dialectical tests (multiple techniques)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a phrase appears inconsistent, apply dialectical methods to resolve it: consider changes of intonation, distinguishing senses, ambiguity, familiar usage, transference (metaphor), and number of possible senses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques listed include: (1) change of intonation; (2) distinguishing (showing different readings/senses in context); (3) pointing to ambiguity; (4) citing familiar/colloquial usage; (5) transference (metaphorical or genus/species shifts); and (6) counting how many senses the word could bear here. Numerous examples (Homeric lines, Empedocles, etc.) illustrate each technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: When literal inconsistency occurs, test whether it is same reference and sense
rubrics_metrics.description: If a passage taken literally is inconsistent, determine whether the same thing is meant in the same reference and sense (in which case the poet is inconsistent) or only so under the critic’s assumptions (in which case the critic errs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the dialectical test: if the apparent contradiction rests on conflating different references or senses, the poet may be vindicated; if not, the inconsistency is the poet’s.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories of critical objection and the range of solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Critical objections fall into five main types—impossible, unnatural, immoral, inconsistent, or inartistic—and there are a set of (twelve enumerated) possible solutions to these objections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The provided roster of solutions includes defenses such as: realistic, conventional/traditional, idealistic treatment; poetry conflicting with another science but excusable if not essential; incidental (not essential) errors; foreign words/dialect usages; metaphorical usage; familiar usage; mistaken sense or intonation; ambiguity; transference; and others. Students should map objections to these solution-formulae.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select form by which art best realizes its purpose; favor unity and concentrated effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose the literary form (Epic vs Tragic) that more effectively realizes the art’s purpose; Tragedy is judged superior because it can realize its ends with greater unity, compression, and intensified gratification (music and spectacle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments for Tragedy: tragic effect can be produced by perusal though performance may enhance it; the compressed product gives more pleasure than a diluted one; tragedy adds music/exhibition to intensify gratification; tragedy often attains greater unity (a romance may contain multiple life‑chapters and feel diffuse). The evaluator should prefer the form that better achieves the intended poetic function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware limits and effects of composite/staged performance on poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: In a stage (composite) performance each art (poetry, acting, music, spectacle) may compromise others; actors or spectacle can distract from or require the poet to abbreviate content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When poetry is combined with acting and music, poetry may be confined to speeches and lyric passages shortened; judges should attribute faults sometimes to actors or inferior execution rather than to the poetic form itself. Conversely, some tragic effects may be better achieved in performance than in mere reading.
